messages.subject: dev=tikz doesn't work
messages.body_plain:

Error : failed to compile <fig_file>.tikz to PDF

I updated the tikzDevice package and knitr to the latest versions, and I believe I have a recent tikz/pgf installation.

Any ideas on how I can debug this?

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] dev=tikz doesn't work
messages.body_plain:
You can open that <fig_file>.tikz and see if you can find anything suspicious.

Or try to compile it to PDF directly by

pdflatex filename.tikz

and see filename.log if there are LaTeX errors.

Yet another thing to mention is be aware of special characters in your
plot, and you might need sanitize=TRUE.

messages.body_plain:
I have been using a custom function for preparing LaTeX output from R
ftables; this has worked without problems up until today, when I moved
to knitr 0.3. After making the expected changes to my document (e.g.
results=tex -> results="tex") I was concerned to find a new error,
generated wherever I have used my custom function. Note that the
output of the function works just fine - everything behaves perfectly
when I insert the generated LaTeX code instead of the function to
generate same. (And when I remove my ftables, the rest of the document
behaves perfectly, so the generation of the LaTeX code for the ftables
is definitely the sticking point).

It seems that such 'Not in outer par mode' errors occur when there is
a floating environment inside some other incompatible environment (or
something like that). Given that there were no such problems under
knitr 0.2, I wonder if this is something that might be fixed in knitr?
Or might there be something that could be changed within the function
(I found it ages ago online but now am not sure who wrote it
originally).

I don't see an option to attach files to this post, so I will send
Yihui separately a MRE, with a sample table, R object, and the code
function.

Thanks in advance for help/suggestions.

Hi Jenny,

I have fixed this problem in the development version; results='tex'
should be safe now. I tested your example and it worked. Please ignore
my previous solution. I also excluded plots from the fragile framed
environments so we will no longer the gray background behind plots.

the same meaning in knitr; the latter was reserved mainly for
compatibility to Sweave, and I think 'tex' is a bad name (Sweave only
had LaTeX in mind when it was invented, but results='tex' really means
do not wrap up the results in any environments like TeX or HTML
environments).

Regards,
Yihui

Things should be cleaner now in the current development version. You
can call render_gfm() before knit(), and knitr will no longer override
your hooks. They work through the whole R session unless you change

knit_hooks$set()  # if you still have other hooks
opts_chunk$set() # set chunk options
opts_knit$set()  # package options
knit()  # ready to knit

All these changes before knit() are permanent in an R session.

messages.body_plain:
I think I understand what you mean, but as we discussed in
https://github.com/yihui/knitr/issues/19 a few months ago, I tend to
keep the number of arguments of a function minimal. On one hand, this
is like ggplot2 vs base R graphics/lattice: you can draw a plot in a
huge function call, or you do your job in small pieces; the procedure
below is the workflow to knit() a document:

pat_xxx()  # set pattern list
render_xxx()  # set output hooks
knit_hooks$set()  # if you still have other hooks
opts_chunk$set() # set chunk options
opts_knit$set()  # package options
knit()  # ready to knit

They are global changes (in terms of the current R session). If you
want to tweak a small number of options inside your document, you can
use \SweaveOpts{} -- this is the second global level (global in terms
of this document, and will be restored when you exit this document).
Then you still have local options in <<>>=; this is the lowest level
-- these options only affect this chunk. I'm not sure if I made these
three levels clear.

On the other hand, I'm kind of pushing users to the reproducible end:
ideally all the above settings can be done inside a document except
pat_xxx(), i.e. make the document as self-contained as possible. But
this will obviously annoy users since it would require them to repeat
the settings in all documents, so there comes the above highest global
settings.

I'm wondering how frequently you need to change all these options, and
why "setting (a large number of) global options outside + (a small
number of) local options inside" is difficult for you.

BTW, I almost always call knitr via Rscript to avoid option/object
clashes, and I group similar types of documents and compile them
together, so I do not need to change all these options/hooks
frequently.

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Briefly speaking, this is just a system() call to metafile2eps.exe
using a chunk hook, and it is very similar to the hook_pdfcrop()
function: https://github.com/yihui/knitr/blob/master/R/hooks.R

Read more about chunk hooks and see if you can DIY:
http://yihui.name/knitr/hooks I can help if you cannot figure it out.

Note knitr does not write the filename extension to the tex output,
e.g. for foo.eps, it only write \includegraphics{foo} instead of
\includegraphics{foo.eps}, therefore all you need to do is to convert
the metafile to eps, and you do not need to worry about the tex file
since it does not need to be changed. LaTeX complained because it
could note find an plot file with an expected extension (wmf is not
supported).

Also note eps does not work with pdflatex, if I remember correctly (I
have not used postscript for a few years, so I may be wrong). You may
still go to pdf finally. So I'm curious what is the particular reason
that you have to use windows metafile?

------

The other lazy approach is to use chunk option include=FALSE to
suppress the output completely, but the plot file will be generated as
usual; then you can insert the file into LyX, and let LyX convert it
for you. In this approach your document is no longer completely
dynamic.

messages.subject: knitr 0.4 is on CRAN
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I pushed a new version of knitr to CRAN last night (Windows users need
to wait for a few more hours); news and changes can be found in:
https://github.com/yihui/knitr/blob/master/NEWS

Most notable changes are:

- package option 'concordance': it is super powerful with RStudio
(currently in its daily build versions); error navigation and Rnw/pdf
sync become extremely easy (you can jump back and forth between source
and output); although Sweave invented it quite a few years ago, it has
always been a half-baked feature; now it is fully functional in
RStudio
- package option 'upload.fun': you can define your own function to
upload images to servers; for 0.3.x users, please note options
'upload' and 'imgur.key' have been removed, per suggestion of
https://github.com/yihui/knitr/issues/173
- chunk option 'autodep': a feature borrowed from weaver package to
set up automatic dependencies among cached chunks

I'm confident to say knitr is almost a strict superset of Sweave now,
which is unexpected to me since I did not plan to implement some
features in the beginning, and I thank you all for sharing practical
experience which has greatly motivated the development. This is my
shameless summary of knitr:

Sweave + cacheSweave + pgfSweave + weaver + R2HTML::RweaveHTML +
highlight::HighlightWeaveLatex + 0.2 * brew + 0.1 * SweaveListingUtils
+ more

I think LaTeX support should be enough, and I will focus more on
HTML/markdown in the next version.

Regards,
Yihui

I feel <!--begin.rcode and end.rcode--> are too long to type, and I

    #re

rb means "r begin", and re is "r end". Or

    code
    #%}

or

    #}}

messages.body_plain:
So I think I worked out a great proof of concept for everything in a
single regular expression.  I made a gist at
https://gist.github.com/5a4448e6f4edd925bbc0 where you can see it but
I will repeat it here.  The idea uses perl regular expressions with
named chunks.  All the patterns combined into one regex so that
matches can be reused.  The look ahead operator defines and end chunk
with out capturing the end chunk.  If the end chunk is ``` then is
match and consumes it.  The named pattern allows for the things to be
extracted by name.  I show how to extract the options and body of each
chunk with the chunks chained together.

Chaining the patterns together into a single regex is powerful because
you can match the same number ticks at the end as at the beginning.
It also has the advantage of being much more explicit of an ending.
This way chained chunks can be either allowed or disallowed as a
pattern.  There was a trick that I had to do to simulate the multiline
option, since I saw no way to turn that on.

``````r
# Test String
s <- "
# header
```knitr chunk
1+1
```knitr cache=T
2+2
```
more documentation
and some more
"

# Define patterns with named chunks for extraction
head <- "(^|(?<=\\n))(?P<ticks>```+)knitr(?P<options>[^\\n]*)"
body <- "(?P<body>.*?)"
end  <- "((?=(?P=ticks)knitr)|(?P=ticks))"

# Combine patterns with newlines between
(pattern <- paste(head, body, end, sep="\\n"))

# extract all matchs
(m <- gregexpr(pattern, s, perl=T))

# Check matches
regmatches(s, m, invert=F)

# extract match start and end points
start  <- attr(m[[1]], "capture.start")
length <- attr(m[[1]], "capture.length")

# Extract options Strings
os <- start[, 'options']
oe <- os + length[, 'options']-1
options <- substring(s, os, oe)

# Extract body strings
bs <- start[, 'body']
be <- os + length[, 'body']-1
body <- substring(s, bs, be)
```````

> So I think I worked out a great proof of concept for everything in a
> single regular expression.  I made a gist at
> https://gist.github.com/5a4448e6f4edd925bbc0 where you can see it but
> I will repeat it here.  The idea uses perl regular expressions with
> named chunks.  All the patterns combined into one regex so that
> matches can be reused.  The look ahead operator defines and end chunk
> with out capturing the end chunk.  If the end chunk is ``` then is
> match and consumes it.  The named pattern allows for the things to be
> extracted by name.  I show how to extract the options and body of each
> chunk with the chunks chained together.
>
> Chaining the patterns together into a single regex is powerful because
> you can match the same number ticks at the end as at the beginning.
> It also has the advantage of being much more explicit of an ending.
> This way chained chunks can be either allowed or disallowed as a
> pattern.  There was a trick that I had to do to simulate the multiline
> option, since I saw no way to turn that on.
>
> ``````r
> # Test String
> s <- "
> # header
> ```knitr chunk
> 1+1
> ```knitr cache=T
> 2+2
> ```
> more documentation
> and some more
> "
>
> # Define patterns with named chunks for extraction
> head <- "(^|(?<=\\n))(?P<ticks>```+)knitr(?P<options>[^\\n]*)"
> body <- "(?P<body>.*?)"
> end  <- "((?=(?P=ticks)knitr)|(?P=ticks))"
>
> # Combine patterns with newlines between
> (pattern <- paste(head, body, end, sep="\\n"))
>
> # extract all matchs
> (m <- gregexpr(pattern, s, perl=T))
>
> # Check matches
> regmatches(s, m, invert=F)
>
> # extract match start and end points
> start  <- attr(m[[1]], "capture.start")
> length <- attr(m[[1]], "capture.length")
>
> # Extract options Strings
> os <- start[, 'options']
> oe <- os + length[, 'options']-1
> options <- substring(s, os, oe)
>
> # Extract body strings
> bs <- start[, 'body']
> be <- os + length[, 'body']-1
> body <- substring(s, bs, be)
> ```````
>

optionally with a makefile is the best approach.  The error that you

messages.body_plain:
I have been running large simulations in code chunks and the results
are used elsewhere in the document.

Because they generate so much data, I don't even want to cache them.
Rather, what I am doing is putting in a "save(...)" at the end of
these chunks which would dump the results into a Rdata file for
reference. Another file I save is a summary data file which I save to
a different Rdata file to be read-in for plotting parts of the
document.

What I would like to do is set "eval=FALSE" to these (memory hogging)
simulation chunks easily.
There are multiple number of these chunks, so changing them to TRUE
when I want to run them is a big pain.

So, when I am ready to rebuild the document from scratch including the
simulations, I can change one thing and run it overnight.

Is there something I can do which would selectively set eval=TRUE or
eval=FALSE for predetermined set of chunks?

Thanks!

just a thought.
Carl
